title: Lille Weather & Climate – Forecasts, Temperature & Packing
content:
There are four distinct seasons in Lille. Winter (December-February) is characterised by average temperatures of around 4-6°C, with minimums potentially dropping to 2-3°C, while maximums rarely exceed 9°C. Spring (March-May) brings gradual warming: the average air temperature rises from 7-8°C in March to 13-14°C in May. Summer (June-August) is the warmest season with average temperatures of 17-19°C, while daytime maximums can reach 22-23°C. Autumn (September-November) is distinguished by a gradual decrease in temperature from 16°C in September to 8°C in November. [...] ## Temperature

The weather in Lille is characterised by a temperate maritime climate with noticeable seasonal temperature changes. The annual temperature range is quite pronounced: the coldest months are typically January, with an average temperature of about 4.8°C (minimum night temperatures can drop to 2.4°C, and daytime maximums reach approximately 7.1°C), and December, where the average temperature is 6.0°C. The warmest months are July and August. In August, the average temperature reaches 19.0°C, with daytime maximums averaging around 23.3°C and night-time minimums around 14.7°C. July is also very warm, with an average temperature of 18.6°C. [...] Average monthly precipitation

## What to Pack

When planning a trip to Lille, it is important to consider the peculiarities of the local climate so that your luggage is packed correctly. The weather in Lille is characterised by moderate temperatures year-round and a high probability of precipitation, even if not always abundant. The number of rainy days is quite high (from 10 to 15 per month), so indispensable items in your suitcase will be a compact umbrella or a light raincoat. Also, be sure to bring comfortable, preferably waterproof, shoes for long walks around the city. The principle of layering in clothing is your best ally, as it will allow you to easily adapt to temperature changes throughout the day, especially in the off-season.

## General Weather Overview

The climate of **Lille**, located in the north of **France**, can be characterised as *temperate maritime*. This means the city does not experience extreme temperature fluctuations throughout the year. The weather here is distinguished by its mildness: winters are usually cool, and summers are warm but rarely exhaustingly hot. Overall, the climate is conducive to a comfortable visit to the city at any time of the year.

There are four distinct seasons in **Lille**. Winter (December-February) is characterised by average temperatures of around 4-6°C, with minimums potentially dropping to 2-3°C, while maximums rarely exceed 9°C. Spring (March-May) brings gradual warming: the average air temperature rises from 7-8°C in March to 13-14°C in May. Summer (June-August) is the warmest season with average temperatures of 17-19°C, while daytime maximums can reach 22-23°C. Autumn (September-November) is distinguished by a gradual decrease in temperature from 16°C in September to 8°C in November.

A characteristic feature of the weather in **Lille** is the fairly even distribution of precipitation throughout the year, although the total monthly amount is small (2-3 mm). However, the number of days with precipitation ("wet days") remains significant throughout the year, varying from 10 to 15 days per month. This suggests that light rain or drizzle can be frequent companions, so tourists should be prepared for changeable weather and carry an umbrella or raincoat, especially during the autumn-winter period and early spring.

# Fall 2025 Forecast Update: Calm Before the Winter Storm

By Author [Andrej Flis](https://www.severe-weather.eu/author/asflis/)

Posted on Published: 21/08/2025

Categories [Long range / seasonal forecast](https://www.severe-weather.eu/category/long-range-2/)

**Meteorological Autumn is just around the corner. The latest seasonal forecasts show clear signs of a weak La Niña leaving an impact on the Fall atmosphere. But its influence will spread on the Winter weather patterns across the Northern Hemisphere, especially North America, with a cold reversal now indicated.**

The tropical Pacific Ocean is already cooling, pointing to the likely return of a weak La Niña in the coming weeks.

This is important because La Niña is well-known for its impact on seasonal weather patterns, even in a weak form. So, before going into the Fall forecasts, we will quickly look at how La Niña works and what its past influence can tell us for the upcoming season, with very interesting cold winter indicators found in the latest data.
